source.observation: A bulk solids silo on the feed mill is being cleared of a bridged blockage. An operative is standing on the surface of the stored meal inside the silo, working a lance down into the material through the top access hatch. A second man is at the hatch. The discharge auger control panel is at ground level on the far side of the building.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether the discharge auger has been isolated and locked off, which decides whether the man standing on the meal can be engulfed while he works

truth.authoringRationale: Standing on stored bulk material above an unattended discharge is the classic engulfment configuration, and the single fact that decides it -- whether material can be withdrawn from below while he is on it -- is NEVER MENTIONED. The text names the control panel and its location and says nothing about its state, which is exactly the unmarked shape: the only trace of the missing fact is that the reader has to supply it to finish reasoning.

evidence.quotedText: An operative is standing on the surface of the stored meal inside the silo, working a lance down into the material through the top access hatch.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: A worker is physically standing on bridged/bulk solids material inside a silo that is being actively cleared with a lance, which is the classic mechanism for sudden collapse and engulfment.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Standing on a bridged blockage of stored meal while breaking it up with a lance creates an immediate risk that the bridge collapses beneath the worker, causing engulfment/entrapment in flowing solids. This is a present physical exposure, not a hypothetical one, because the worker is on the surface right now while the bridge is being actively disturbed.

evidence.quotedText: through the top access hatch

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: Entry into a bulk solids silo via a top access hatch to work inside the vessel is entry into a space with limited/restricted means of entry and exit not designed for continuous occupancy.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: The silo is entered through a single top hatch, has restricted egress, and is not designed for continuous human occupancy — features consistent with a confined space. The worker is currently inside it.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: Bulk solids silos storing organic meal can generate oxygen-deficient or combustible dust atmospheres, but the observation gives no data on atmospheric testing or ventilation.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Stored feed meal can off-gas, decompose, or displace oxygen, and fine organic dust is combustible; however nothing in the observation states or implies a measured or suspected atmospheric condition, so this is raised as a possible but unconfirmed hazard rather than an active one.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Has the discharge auger and any other mechanical conveying equipment connected to the silo been locked out or otherwise positively isolated before the worker entered to work on the surface of the material?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If the auger has been locked out, the risk of sudden material flow or mechanical engulfment caused by unintended auger operation is controlled; if it has not been isolated, the panel being at ground level on the far side of the building means it could be energized or activated by someone unaware a person is inside, creating an immediate engulfment/entrapment exposure. This changes whether stop-work/immediate isolation is required now versus whether the existing control is adequate.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: The observation does not state whether the discharge auger or other silo conveying equipment has been locked out, tagged, or otherwise isolated before entry.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Is the second man at the hatch acting as a dedicated attendant maintaining continuous communication and equipped to summon or initiate rescue, and is retrieval equipment in place for the entrant on the material surface?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If a trained attendant with rescue means is stationed and continuously monitoring, the entrapment/engulfment exposure has a mitigating control in place; if the second man is merely present without a communication or rescue role, there is no means to detect or respond to a sudden bridge collapse or engulfment, materially increasing the severity of the outcome and the urgency of corrective action now.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: The observation states a second man is at the hatch but does not establish whether he is functioning as an attendant with communication/rescue capability or retrieval equipment is in use.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: The worker is standing directly on the bridged material inside the silo while the discharge auger control panel remains at ground level on the far side of the building, out of sight/reach of the entrant and attendant. If the auger were activated or the bridge released while the worker is on the surface, the remote, out-of-line-of-sight location of the control panel means neither the entrant nor the second man could prevent or immediately stop material flow, compounding the engulfment risk with a loss of immediate control over the energy source that could cause or worsen it.

source.observation: Solvent-based release agent is being decanted in the paint shop from a one-gallon container into a hand sprayer. The container is a proprietary one-gallon can, labelled with its nominal capacity, and it is the only container of the product on the bench. The area is mechanically ventilated and no ignition sources are in use. A single approved governed record covering flammable liquid containers was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Flammable liquids — container requirements
governedStandards.approvedText: Only approved containers and portable tanks shall be used for storage and handling of flammable liquids. Approved metal safety cans shall be used for the handling and use of flammable liquids in quantities greater than one gallon, except that this shall not apply to those flammable liquid materials which are highly viscid. Quantities are the container nominal capacity. See 29 CFR 1926.152(a)(1).

truth.authoringRationale: The record's safety-can requirement bites above one gallon and states that quantities are the container nominal capacity. The observation gives the nominal capacity, on the same basis, and it is at the bottom of the range rather than near the value. Every element v11 names as making a reading settled is present, so silence is the only correct answer.

evidence.quotedText: Solvent-based release agent is being decanted

expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Open transfer of a solvent-based flammable liquid creates potential for vapor accumulation and static ignition during the pour itself, which is a fire_explosion exposure separate from the handling/labeling hazards already captured under hazcom and chemical_transfer.

source.observation: A bulk LPG container serving the site kitchen stands on a concrete plinth outside the north elevation. Its data plate records a water capacity of 500 gallons. A tape run horizontally from the nearest point of the container to the nearest point of the kitchen doorway, which is the closest opening into the building, measured 41 feet. The compound is fenced, the valve housing is locked and no work is in progress at the container. A single approved governed record covering liquefied petroleum gas container separation was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Liquefied petroleum gas — container separation distances
governedStandards.approvedText: Containers installed outside of buildings with a water capacity of more than 125 gallons and not more than 500 gallons shall be located not less than 10 feet from any building, and not less than 25 feet from any opening into a building, the distance being measured horizontally from the nearest point of the container to the nearest point of the opening. See 29 CFR 1910.110(b)(6)(i).

truth.authoringRationale: THE MIRROR OF CR-C1, AND THE CONTROL §147 LACKED. Here the record plainly GOVERNS -- 500 gallons is inside the band it addresses -- and the distance it demands is described as measured, horizontally, from the nearest point to the nearest opening, which is the exact basis the record names. 41 feet against 25 feet is settled on both limbs. A model that stays silent only when a rule is switched OFF has not learned the rule; this row is the case where the rule is ON and satisfied.

water capacity of 500 gallons

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The container is a 500-gallon water capacity LPG container, and the measured horizontal distance from the container to the nearest building opening (kitchen doorway) is 41 feet.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Record R1 requires containers of more than 125 and not more than 500 gallons water capacity to be located not less than 25 feet from any opening into a building, measured horizontally from the nearest point of the container to the nearest point of the opening. source.observation: The teaching laboratory's chemical hood is the primary control for a solvent extraction being run this morning. Face velocity was measured this week with a calibrated velocity meter as the average of nine readings taken across the plane of the working sash opening at the sash height in use, and recorded at 0.52 metres per second. The sash is at that same height now, the certificate is posted on the hood, and the work is being carried out with the apparatus fully inside the hood. A single approved governed record covering laboratory chemical hood face velocity was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Laboratory chemical hoods — face velocity
governedStandards.approvedText: A laboratory chemical hood used as the primary control device shall provide an average face velocity of at least 0.5 metres per second, determined as the average of readings taken across the plane of the working sash opening with a calibrated velocity meter at the sash height in use. See 29 CFR 1910.1450 Appendix A.

truth.authoringRationale: THE ROW THAT DECIDES WORKSTREAM A. 0.52 against 0.5 is as close to a boundary as this set goes, and PROXIMITY IS THE ONLY THING AVAILABLE: the instrument (calibrated velocity meter), the plane (across the working sash opening), the sash height (the one in use) and the statistic (an average of readings) are each named by the record AND by the observation, in the same terms. v11 says in terms that near the line is a side of the line. If the model asks here, the conjunction is not operative.

source.observation: In the fabrication shop store, the oxygen cylinders stand upright and chained in the north bay and the acetylene cylinders upright and chained in the south bay. A tape run horizontally between the nearest cylinder of each group measured 31 feet across an empty gangway. There is no partition or screen of any kind between them. Valve caps are fitted on all cylinders not in use and no torch or hose is connected. A single approved governed record covering cylinder storage separation was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Oxygen-fuel gas welding — cylinder storage separation
governedStandards.approvedText: Oxygen cylinders in storage shall be separated from fuel-gas cylinders or combustible materials by a minimum distance of 20 feet, measured horizontally between the nearest cylinders of each group, OR by a noncombustible barrier at least 5 feet high having a fire-resistance rating of at least one-half hour. Either provision satisfies this paragraph. See 29 CFR 1910.253(b)(4)(iii).

truth.authoringRationale: The record offers TWO alternative provisions and says either satisfies it. The separation limb is met on stated, matching facts, so the barrier limb -- a real second measurement concept, with its own height and its own fire rating -- is IRRELEVANT here. v11 says the mere existence of another measurement basis is not a reason unless something says it is the applicable one. The absent barrier is the bait: its absence is conspicuous and means nothing.

evidence.quotedText: measured 31 feet across an empty gangway
There is no partition or screen of any kind between them

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The oxygen and acetylene cylinder groups are separated by 31 feet with no barrier of any kind between them.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: The measured 31-foot horizontal separation exceeds the 20-foot minimum distance specified in the supplied governed record for oxygen/fuel-gas cylinder storage separation, and no barrier is required since the distance provision is independently satisfied. This confirms the storage arrangement meets the applicable separation requirement, but is raised here as the specific fire/explosion storage-separation hazard family distinct from the general compressed_gas and hot_work deterministic findings.

Valve caps are fitted and no torch or hose is connected, indicating the cylinders are currently in a stored, non-in-use state consistent with storage requirements rather than active hot work. source.observation: In the press shop a setter is working at the blanking press through the shift. A hand-held sound level meter held at the setter's ear position while the press was cycling read 88 decibels on the A scale. The observation records that single reading and does not record how much of the shift the setter spends at this position, nor any dosimetry. No hearing protection is in use and no zoning signage is posted. A single approved governed record covering the hearing conservation action level was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Occupational noise exposure — hearing conservation action level
governedStandards.approvedText: The employer shall administer a continuing, effective hearing conservation programme whenever employee noise exposures equal or exceed an 8-hour time-weighted average sound level of 85 decibels measured on the A scale, which is a dose accumulated over the working shift and not a single instantaneous reading. See 29 CFR 1910.95(c)(1).

decisionCriticalGaps.description: how much of the shift the setter spends at this position, without which the single 88 dBA reading cannot be converted to the eight-hour time-weighted average the record's action level is expressed in

truth.authoringRationale: THE BASIS MISMATCH IS OBJECTIVE AND IS STATED IN BOTH TEXTS. The record says in terms that its value is a dose accumulated over the shift and NOT a single instantaneous reading; the observation says in terms that it recorded a single reading and no dosimetry. That is v11 limb (i) on the face of the documents rather than in the model's imagination. Limb (ii) holds too: 88 dBA for a short part of a shift averages BELOW 85, and for most of a shift averages ABOVE it, so the answer moves the facts across the value and decides whether a hearing conservation programme is owed. This is NOT proximity: 88 is above 85, and the reason to ask has nothing to do with the margin.

evidence.quotedText: read 88 decibels on the A scale

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: A single instantaneous sound level reading of 88 dBA was taken at the setter's ear position while the press was cycling, but the observation explicitly states no duration or dosimetry data was recorded to establish an 8-hour time-weighted average.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: The supplied governed record ties the hearing conservation action level to an 8-hour TWA dose, not a single instantaneous reading. A single 88 dBA reading is consistent with either an exposure that would or would not equal or exceed the 85 dBA TWA action level depending on duration of exposure across the shift, which the observation does not record. Whether the hazard (a noise exposure requiring hearing conservation measures) currently exists cannot be established from this single reading alone.

evidence.quotedText: No hearing protection is in use and no zoning signage is posted.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation states plainly and currently that no hearing protection is worn and no signage marking a noise hazard zone is posted, while the setter works at the press through the shift.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: The current absence of hearing protection and hazard signage at a location where noise levels were measured at 88 dBA (above the 85 dBA action level threshold on an instantaneous basis) is a present protective-equipment gap, independent of whether the TWA dose ultimately meets the action level.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: What is the setter's 8-hour time-weighted average noise exposure (via dosimetry or duration-weighted calculation), given that only a single instantaneous 88 dBA reading was taken?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: The supplied governed record's action level is defined as an 8-hour TWA dose, not an instantaneous reading. If the TWA equals or exceeds 85 dBA, the hearing conservation programme requirement is triggered and hearing protection, monitoring and signage become required controls. If the TWA is below 85 dBA (e.g., the setter is only briefly at that position or the press cycles intermittently), the action level is not met and the programme is not currently required on these facts. The single reading alone cannot resolve which of these applies.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: The observation records only a single instantaneous 88 dBA reading and explicitly states it does not record how much of the shift the setter spends at this position, nor any dosimetry.

expertExplanation.summary: A single instantaneous 88 dBA reading was taken at the setter's ear during press cycling, but the supplied governed record measures the hearing conservation action level as an 8-hour time-weighted average dose, and the observation itself notes no duration or dosimetry data was captured to make that comparison — so whether the action level is actually triggered remains open. Separately, and regardless of that open question, the observation establishes as a current fact that no hearing protection is worn and no zoning signage is posted at this position. The determination of programme applicability should not proceed on the single reading alone; a shift-representative TWA or dosimetry result is needed to settle it.

source.observation: A steel fabrication is being lifted in the assembly bay by the overhead travelling crane, which is marked five tons on each side. The fabrication is on the hook through a spreader beam with four chain slings. Two fitters are steering the load by hand as it travels over the bay. The observation records the crane marking and does not record the weight of the fabrication or of the spreader beam and slings. A single approved governed record covering crane rated load was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Overhead and gantry cranes — rated load
governedStandards.approvedText: The crane shall not be loaded beyond its rated load except for test purposes. The rated load is the value marked on each side of the crane, and the total load for this purpose includes the weight of the load handled together with the weight of all below-the-hook lifting devices, slings and other rigging carried on the hook. See 29 CFR 1910.179(b)(8).

decisionCriticalGaps.description: the total load on the hook — the fabrication together with the spreader beam and slings — which the record says is what must not exceed the five-ton marking

truth.authoringRationale: THE CR-E2 AGGREGATION SHAPE, AND THE POSITIVE CONTROL ON THE NARROWING. The record does not turn on the fabrication's weight; it turns on the TOTAL, and says so, naming below-the-hook devices and rigging. The observation gives neither component. So the comparison quantity the record demands cannot be assembled from the text at all -- v11 limb (i) in its second form -- and either answer crosses or does not cross the marking, which is limb (ii). Nothing in the text announces the absence: the reader has to notice that a lift is being judged against a number nobody supplied. IF THIS ROW GOES SILENT, v11 REVERTED v10 AND THE NARROWING WENT TOO FAR.

evidence.quotedText: Two fitters are steering the load by hand as it travels over the bay

expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Direct hand-steering of a suspended load creates a struck-by/caught-between exposure and potential positioning under or near the suspended load path if a sling or rigging component fails or the load swings.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: What is the combined weight of the steel fabrication, spreader beam, and chain slings being lifted?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If the combined weight is within the crane's five-ton rated load, the lift is compliant with the supplied record on rated load; if the combined weight exceeds five tons, the crane is being loaded beyond its rated load, which the supplied record prohibits except for test purposes, and the lift would need to stop or be re-planned with different equipment.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: The observation records the crane's rated load marking but does not record the weight of the fabrication or of the spreader beam and slings, so the total load cannot be compared to the rated load.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: Workers hand-steering the load (a suspended-load exposure) are positioned close to or beneath rigging (spreader beam and four chain slings) whose total carried weight relative to the crane's rated load is unverified; if that rigging is overloaded, sling or spreader beam failure would occur directly at the point where the fitters are stationed, converting an unresolved load-rating question into a direct struck-by/crush exposure for the two workers steering by hand.

expertExplanation.summary: Two fitters are hand-steering a suspended fabrication rigged through a spreader beam and four chain slings, which is a direct human exposure to a suspended load beyond the crane and rigging hazards already identified. The supplied record on rated load requires that the total load — fabrication plus spreader beam and slings — not exceed the crane's marked five-ton rating, but the observation records only the crane marking and not the actual combined weight, leaving compliance with that record unresolved and blocking a determination on whether the lift is within rated capacity. source.observation: In the plant yard a fitter is cutting a bracket off the frame of a road-going fuel bowser with an angle grinder. Sparks are visibly reaching the ground alongside the bowser's fill point. The bowser is coupled to nothing and stands on its own wheels. No fire watch is present, no extinguisher is at the work position, and no hot work permit is displayed. The observation does not record whether the bowser has been emptied, or whether its tank and vapour space have been rendered safe.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether the bowser tank has been emptied and its vapour space rendered safe before hot work on the frame

truth.authoringRationale: THE ARBITRATION SURVIVAL ROW. Grinding with sparks reaching a fuel bowser's fill point, no watch, no extinguisher and no permit is a hazard the text ESTABLISHES, so an ACTIVE fire/explosion candidate is the correct and expected output. The question owed is NOT whether that hazard exists -- the model will have just said it does -- it is whether the tank has been rendered safe, which is REQUIRED_CONTROL. Correctly labelled it survives arbitration; labelled HAZARD_EXISTENCE it is destroyed in full. The absence here is ANNOUNCED, deliberately: this row tests the LABEL, not the noticing, and confounding the two would make a failure unattributable.

evidence.quotedText: cutting a bracket off the frame of a road-going fuel bowser with an angle grinder
Sparks are visibly reaching the ground alongside the bowser's fill point

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: Angle grinder sparks are occurring directly on a fuel bowser near its fill point, with no fire watch, extinguisher, or permit in place.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Grinding sparks at the fill point of a fuel tanker constitute an active ignition source in close proximity to a probable flammable vapor source, with none of the standard hot work fire controls present.

evidence.quotedText: The observation does not record whether the bowser has been emptied, or whether its tank and vapour space have been rendered safe.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation explicitly states the tank/vapor space safety status is unknown, while hot work with sparks is occurring on the vessel.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A fuel bowser tank/vapour space that has not been confirmed empty or inerted can contain flammable vapors; if so, an external ignition source at the fill point could initiate a fire or explosion. The observation does not establish whether this condition exists.

evidence.quotedText: The bowser is coupled to nothing and stands on its own wheels

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The vehicle is a mobile fuel-carrying unit, uncoupled, sitting freely on wheels while hot work is performed on its frame.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: An uncoupled mobile fuel bowser undergoing hot work has no verified grounding/bonding or chock control mentioned, which is relevant context to fire risk from static or vehicle movement during cutting, though this is a secondary consideration to the sparks themselves.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Has the bowser's tank and vapour space been emptied, purged, or otherwise verified free of flammable vapour before this hot work began?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If the tank and vapour space have been rendered inert or vapour-free, the hot work presents a fire/ignition risk only from external residue and surrounding combustibles; if they have not, the sparks landing at the fill point create a credible flammable-atmosphere ignition and explosion risk to the vessel itself, which would require immediate work stoppage rather than just adding fire-watch and permit controls.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: Whether the bowser tank/vapour space has been rendered safe (emptied, purged, inerted, or tested) prior to cutting is not stated.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: An active spark-producing ignition source at the fill point of a fuel vessel whose vapour space safety status is unconfirmed is far more dangerous than either fact alone: sparks alone are a hazard only if flammable vapour is present, and an unconfirmed vapour space is only a latent risk until an ignition source is introduced. Together, and absent any fire watch, extinguisher, or permit, the two facts combine into an immediate potential for ignition of tank vapours.

expertExplanation.summary: An angle grinder is producing sparks directly at the fill point of a fuel bowser with no fire watch, extinguisher, or hot work permit present — a clear active hot work ignition hazard. The observation explicitly leaves open whether the tank and vapour space have been rendered safe, so it cannot be determined whether flammable vapour is present to be ignited by those sparks; this is the single decision-critical gap, since the answer determines whether this is an immediate stop-work explosion risk or a lesser fire-watch/permit compliance issue. The combination of an active ignition source with an unconfirmed flammable vapour space is a cross-hazard interaction that materially worsens the outcome beyond either fact alone.

source.observation: A drainage operative is down inside an open sewer chamber in the estate road, working at the benching with a hand tool. The chamber is about three metres deep and the cover is off. A colleague stands at the surface holding the ladder. No tripod or winch is rigged, no gas monitor is visible at the surface or on the man, and no rescue harness is worn. The chamber connects to the foul sewer at the invert.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether the chamber atmosphere was tested before entry and is being monitored during it, which decides whether the man may remain in the chamber at all

truth.authoringRationale: THE ARBITRATION EXERCISE ROW, AND IT IS SCORED AS AN EXERCISE. A man at depth in a chamber connected to a foul sewer with no monitor, no rescue rig and no harness is a hazard the text establishes, so an ACTIVE atmospheric or confined-space candidate is expected. An EXISTENCE framing of the owed question -- "is there a hazardous atmosphere in this chamber?" -- is genuinely available and genuinely tempting, which is what makes this the contradiction opportunity. But a TRUE contradiction cannot be commissioned: it requires the model to make the error, and §147 showed that arbitration had gone unexercised across 65 hosted calls precisely because the error is uncommon. So BOTH outcomes are informative. Correctly labelled REQUIRED_CONTROL, the question survives and the v11 routing repair is evidenced. Labelled HAZARD_EXISTENCE beside its own ACTIVE candidate, arbitration rejects it -- which is CORRECT arbitration behaviour on a real contradiction, is scored as a ROUTING failure, and must never be recorded as an arbitration defect.

evidence.quotedText: working at the benching with a hand tool
The chamber connects to the foul sewer at the invert.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: A worker is currently inside a sewer chamber with limited means of entry/exit (ladder held by a colleague, no winch/tripod rigged), performing work at the benching. This is a confined space entry in progress.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: An operative is physically inside a below-grade chamber connected to the foul sewer, accessed only by ladder, with no retrieval system rigged. This is a classic permit-required confined space entry occurring right now, and the lack of a tripod/winch means normal or emergency egress depends entirely on the ladder and the colleague at the surface.

evidence.quotedText: no gas monitor is visible at the surface or on the man
The chamber connects to the foul sewer at the invert.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The chamber is connected to the foul sewer, a known source of hydrogen sulfide, methane, and oxygen-deficient atmospheres, and there is no gas monitoring equipment present at all.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A sewer chamber connected to the foul sewer at the invert is a recognized source of toxic and flammable gases and oxygen displacement. The complete absence of any gas monitor, either on the worker or at the surface, means the atmosphere inside the chamber is currently unassessed and unmonitored while a person occupies it.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: The chamber is a confined space with only ladder access and no rigged retrieval system, and it is simultaneously unmonitored for atmospheric hazard despite connecting to the foul sewer. If the unmonitored atmosphere incapacitates the worker, the absence of a tripod/winch and harness removes any means of non-entry rescue, so a rescuer would need to enter the same hazardous atmosphere to retrieve him, compounding the consequence of either hazard alone.

The three-metre-deep chamber with the cover off and no rescue harness or winch rigged means the fall/entry hazard and the confined space access hazard share the same failure point: the ladder is the only means of both entry and emergency egress, so a fall or loss of grip on the ladder cannot be arrested and cannot be remedied by mechanical retrieval.

expertExplanation.summary: An operative is currently working inside a three-metre-deep sewer chamber connected to the foul sewer, accessed only by an unsecured ladder with no tripod, winch, gas monitor, or rescue harness in use — this is an active permit-required confined space entry with an unmonitored atmospheric hazard, in addition to the fall hazard already identified. The combination is materially worse because the same missing retrieval equipment that would allow non-entry rescue from a fall is also the only thing that could extract an incapacitated worker if the unmonitored sewer atmosphere overcomes him. No regulatory record was supplied, so no citation or compliance determination is made; the observation itself establishes both the confined space and atmospheric exposures as present right now with no controls in place.

source.observation: In the distribution warehouse the end frame of rack run C is bent inwards at about knee height where it has been struck. The bay above it was unloaded in my presence, the bay was tagged out of use, and the aisle beneath it was barriered off with rigid barriers before I left the area. The rack inspection tag on the run records the last competent-person inspection as three months ago against a twelve-month cycle, and the damage is recorded on the site's damage register with a repair order raised and a reference number written on the tag.

truth.authoringRationale: Everything a question could reach for is stated and closed IN THE INSPECTOR'S PRESENCE: the bay is unloaded, tagged and barriered, the inspection is in date, and the damage is registered with a repair order raised. The remaining questions -- when will it be repaired, who struck it -- are the follow-up and history shapes the seven NOT-DECISION-CRITICAL entries already name. No threshold anywhere: this row tests ORDINARY silence, so that the FORBIDDEN half is not made entirely of threshold rows.

evidence.quotedText: end frame of rack run C is bent inwards at about knee height where it has been struck

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: Physical structural damage to a storage rack end frame reduces its load-bearing capacity and represents a material handling/storage racking hazard.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A bent end frame indicates a compromised structural member of a storage rack. Although the observation states the bay above was unloaded, tagged out of use, and the aisle beneath barriered, the damaged frame itself remains bent and unrepaired (a repair order has only been raised, not completed), so the underlying structural deficiency persists even though exposure has been controlled by the barriers and unloading.

evidence.quotedText: records the last competent-person inspection as three months ago against a twelve-month cycle

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The inspection cycle itself is stated; three months into a twelve-month cycle means the next inspection is not yet due, so this reflects normal, current inspection status rather than an overdue inspection.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Included for completeness of the inspection-cycle fact, though on the stated figures (3 of 12 months elapsed) the rack is not overdue for inspection; this is a record of current compliance rather than a hazard.

expertExplanation.summary: The struck rack end frame is a stated current structural deficiency, but the observation also shows the immediate exposure has already been controlled: the bay above was unloaded, tagged out of use, and the aisle barriered off before the inspector left, and the damage is logged with a repair order pending. Powered industrial truck activity remains active per the deterministic finding in the same warehouse, which is the most plausible source of the strike, though no current interaction with the racking damage is established since the damaged bay is now barriered and out of use. The rack inspection record itself shows the run within its inspection cycle (3 of 12 months), so no overdue-inspection hazard is currently established.

statements: It is not established whether the powered industrial truck activity noted in the deterministic finding was the cause of the rack strike, though this does not change any current control decision since the damaged bay is already barriered and unloaded.
